newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bank inquiry rejects S&L-type danger.
newsitem.headline: Australia bank inquiry rejects S&L-type danger.

text.p: A member of the Wallis committee reviewing Australia's financial system on Sunday rejected criticism of its findings by Commonwealth Bank of Australia managing director David Murray as "almost absurd".

Jeff Carmichael said the committee was surprised by Murray's warning last week that proposed changes to Australia's system of prudential regulation could lead to U.S. savings and loan type collapses and accused him of scaremongering.
"I think it is an almost absurd comparison and one that doesn't do the credibility of his position much good at all," Carmichael said on the Nine Network's Business Sunday programme.

Murray last week launched the first major attack on the Wallis report since its release earlier this month, criticising plans to open up the banking payments system to greater competition and strip the Reserve Bank of Australia of its prudential supervision role.
Carmichael said there was no suggestion of lowering Australia's prudential standards.
"None of the characteristics of the savings and loans situation are present in this system that we have recommended," he said.

"Nor for that matter are they present in the system we have at the moment for both banks and non-banks," he added. "We have a much greater focus on risk management, on capital and none of the prescriptions that led to the problems in the U.S.."

At present the Reserve Bank requires banks and others with banking licences to meet strict prudential requirements on capital reserves and stops non-banks from issuing cheques or allowing them access to the overnight payments system.

The inquiry, headed by businessman Stan Wallis, recommended that non-banks such as pension funds, building societies and even telecommunications groups be allowed access to the payments system and be covered by a single new body called the Australian Prudential Regulation Commission.
Carmichael said the idea was for all institutions to be on the same playing field and meet the same regulatory requirements.
"It is up to the regulator to make sure there is some uniformity or some minimum standard in that prudential basis of all those institutions that are allowed to offer deposits," he said.
"We have taken the view that there is nothing special about banks."
Carmichael said Murray was "very conservative, he's very cosy where he is".
Asked if Murray's comments were scare mongering, Carmichael said: "I very much think so".
